readings.title: Counting birds on a tidal flat
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Volunteers counted shorebirds from a public path. Their totals varied widely even on days when the birds seemed equally numerous. The main obstacle was counts made at different tide levels. A rising tide gathered birds together while low water spread them across distant mud. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a count schedule linked to tide tables. Experienced observers chose safe fixed points and recorded visibility with each count. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated timing explained much of the variation. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced comparable counts at agreed tidal stages. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: wildlife records need consistent conditions. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in counting birds on a tidal flat, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Litter after a beach festival
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A seaside town cleaned its beach after a festival. Volunteers collected many cups but could not tell where most waste came from. The main obstacle was cleanup bags without useful categories. The total weight combined food packaging, fishing material and older litter. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a simple sorted collection trial. Teams counted items by type while following safe handling rules. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated drink containers rose sharply near exits. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced more refill points and bins beside departure routes. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: prevention improves when waste has a source. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in litter after a beach festival, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Protecting a dune path
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Visitors crossed sand dunes to reach a quiet beach. A wooden path existed, but people often left it near the final turn. The main obstacle was a path that appeared to end early. From the usual approach, the last section was hidden by tall grass. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used observations of visitor choices. Rangers recorded where people stepped off and checked whether the route remained visible. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated a clearer final section reduced shortcuts. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a visible path marker and small repair to the boards. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: conservation routes must be easy to follow. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in protecting a dune path, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining a sea-grass restoration area
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A harbour group marked a sea-grass restoration zone. Some boat users thought the markers prohibited all activity across the bay. The main obstacle was boundary signs that looked broader than the rule. The first notice showed the protected area but not the open route around it. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a map review with local boat users. The group compared the marked zone with real navigation choices and conservation advice. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated a clear open route reduced misunderstanding. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised map with both protected and permitted areas. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: environmental rules work better when boundaries are clear. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in explaining a sea-grass restoration area, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the coastal observation programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about coastal ecology and public participation, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关海岸生态与公众参与的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the coastal stewardship team suggesting a practical change to the coastal observation programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the coastal observation programme. People have noticed counts made at different tide levels, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
